title: The Python GIL and Free-Threaded Python

questions.question: A Python service with a 64-thread pool runs at 105 percent CPU on a 16-core machine while handling pure-Python work. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The thread pool is too small for the number of cores
The GIL lets only one thread execute bytecode at a time
The operating system has pinned the process to one core
Python threads are green threads that never use a second core
questions.explanation: Python threads are real OS threads, but on the standard build only the one holding the GIL runs bytecode, so CPU-bound Python saturates roughly one core regardless of thread count. More threads would not help, and OS pinning would show a different pattern across processes.

questions.question: Which of these does the GIL actually guarantee on the standard CPython build?
options: balance += amount completes without another thread interleaving
A check of the balance followed by a debit runs as one unit
A single list.append never corrupts the list's internal structure
Writes by one thread become visible to other threads in program order
questions.explanation: The GIL protects the interpreter's own structures: reference counts and the C-level operations on containers. A single append is one such operation. Compound statements are several bytecodes with possible switch points between them, and the language reference makes no visibility promise; the lock handoff happens to provide one, which is not the same thing.

questions.question: Four threads hash forty 10 MB files with hashlib and finish nearly four times faster than one thread. Why does this not contradict the GIL?
options: The C implementation releases the GIL for the duration of each large hash
hashlib is implemented in Python but uses vectorised bytecode
The GIL is only acquired for I/O, not for CPU-bound computation
Each thread was silently started as a separate process
questions.explanation: C extensions can drop the GIL around long computations (Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS), and hashlib does so for buffers above about 2 KB, so the hashing runs on four cores while Python bytecode remains serialised. The GIL is held during ordinary bytecode execution, including CPU-bound Python, which is exactly the case where threads do not help.

questions.question: A service mixes one CPU-bound thread with twenty I/O-bound threads in one process. What does the convoy effect predict?
options: The CPU-bound thread speeds up because it is rarely interrupted
The interpreter raises the switch interval automatically to compensate
The I/O-bound threads starve the CPU-bound one completely
I/O-bound requests gain latency of up to a switch interval per GIL reacquisition
questions.explanation: When an I/O-bound thread's socket becomes ready it needs the GIL for a few microseconds, but the CPU-bound thread holds it for the whole 5 ms interval, so every I/O thread waits behind it on every wake-up. The CPU-bound thread does not get faster; the I/O threads get slower, which is why CPU-bound work belongs in a separate process.

questions.question: A team moves from one JVM to sixteen Python worker processes. Which consequence is a direct result of the process model rather than of the GIL?
options: Bytecode from different requests can no longer run in parallel
Reference counting becomes slower because of atomic operations
The in-process rate limiter becomes sixteen independent counters
The switch interval must be reduced to keep latency acceptable
questions.explanation: Processes share nothing by default, so every in-process resource (caches, counters, pools, loaded models) is duplicated per worker; a per-merchant limit of 100 silently becomes 1,600. Parallelism is restored by the process model, not lost; atomic reference counting is a free-threaded build property, not a process-model one.

questions.question: Code that was correct under the GIL because it used threading.Lock around every read-modify-write is moved to the free-threaded 3.13 build. What changes?
options: It must be rewritten because Lock no longer serialises threads
It stays correct; code that relied on the GIL by accident is what breaks
It becomes incorrect because biased reference counting reorders writes
It fails to import until every lock is replaced with a per-object lock
questions.explanation: The free-threaded build keeps the interpreter safe with per-object locks and biased reference counting, and threading.Lock works exactly as before. What it removes is the accidental protection the GIL gave to unlocked compound operations like a bare += or a check-then-act, which now lose updates routinely instead of rarely.
